491.history: Coal-breakers of the central diggings settled below the gate of Taigh na Fèithe, in the first years of the age, and Taigh na Fèithe above them kept Leabhar a' Chùraim, Crom's stone in its inner room, and the lamp in the niche that was never let go out. The custodians counted Rolla nan Deònach against the book here in the third year, nine days at the long table, and found one hearth in five of the coal-right meant to go; here they ruled one sealed measure of coal to each hull that should be ready, and the boy-clerk Donnchadh mac Thormoid made the fair copy at fifteen and began, at thirty, the count of years from An Diosal that the crown took up after him. Na Seachd Taighean were sworn before Crom's stone in LE 55 and drew their galleries by lot in the hall in LE 109. Eachann Briseadair's household built the first stone house below the gate, and the row became a town with its own well, smith and reeve in his lifetime. Eilidh Dhubh's tracts were burned in Taigh na Fèithe yard in LE 484; Raghnall Ruadh refused the handful to the shires that stood against him from its store in LE 558, and Riaghailt an Teallaich was drafted in the same yard seven years later. Dòmhnall Ruadh joined the crown to the mastery of Taigh na Fèithe, and was buried at his own wish in a worked-out gallery with an unlit lamp at his head. Queen Gormshuil rode up to the winter burning here in LE 1,795, as she had every winter of her reign, and nothing more is told.
491.known_for: Taigh na Fèithe and Leabhar a' Chùraim

123.history: The small village in the hills a short way from Muileann dhearg sits over the galleries of the vein. An earth tremor in LE 379 cracked three of its wells and brought down a byre; the custodians sent men into the galleries below and found the deep workings untouched, and gave the village stone from their own surplus to raise the byre again, a kindness it did not forget. A second tremor in LE 929 brought down a gallery on fourteen of the custodians' own labourers in the small hours of the morning shift. Taigh na Fèithe closed the gallery rather than dig the dead free, and set a stone at its mouth with the fourteen names cut in the order they went down, the youngest a boy of thirteen, the oldest a woman forty years at the same gallery; households of the mountain leave small stones at its foot on the day of the fall.

354.history: The town eight miles from Muileann dhearg below the mountain was a custodians' town of Clann Raghnaill, whose households kept galleries there. The hosts of Catrìona nic Aonghais and Dùghall Garbh, joined for the purpose, met Raghnall Ruadh below it in LE 560, and Raghnall fell on the field; the next morning his own custodians struck the seal from Taigh na Fèithe store without waiting to be told who now held the mountain. Dùghall took a cut below the arm there that he hid from his physicians and died of it. Three centuries later the heads of Na Seachd Taighean, sitting five years at Taigh na Fèithe to choose a king, spoke the name of Dòmhnall Ruadh of Muileann chrom, who kept three galleries there, and he spent his first night as king naming which of his neighbours he trusted to measure them honestly in his absence. He came back as king to settle a boundary between two households by asking each one's oldest member where they had played as children.
354.known_for: the battle that ended Raghnall Ruadh's refusal, and the mountain's own king

273.history: The walled town near Taigh na Fèithe is the hall of Clann Fhearchair. Fearchar mac Lachlainn was born here, the elder son, and bound as a boy to a custodian's household for seven years while his younger brother Iain was kept at home to learn the hall; when the houses chose Fearchar king in LE 182, he kept his court part of each year here that he might take counsel of Taigh na Fèithe without a journey, and Iain kept Clann Fhearchair's hall when the court was at the capital. The brothers' letters across every season of the double court were gathered here into one leaf-book, boundary disputes beside a long complaint about the capital's cooking. Dùghall Garbh held his following here in the years before Cogadh nan Trì Tagraichean, and died here of the wound he took at Muileann chrom, his last words asking whether Taigh na Fèithe gates stood open. In the thirteenth century masons of Ceann leathan began to buy the veined white stone of the hills above the town, and its quarries were worked from then on.
273.known_for: the double court, and the hall of Clann Fhearchair

67.history: The granary town south of the mountain kept the crown's stores. In the grain strife of LE 37 its reeve, Tormod mac Coinnich, who remembered a store-house swept empty behind a smiling reeve when he was seven, barred the granary doors and set a watch of four on them through Samhnas, Dubhlas and the black months, turning away every petitioner until a single rider came in Sìolach with a word that the grain might move; how the strife was settled he was never told. The middle pier of its bridge was rebuilt in stone in LE 46. Sìleas's firlot settled its first quarrel here, a carter and a miller measured true before the crowd their shouting drew. In LE 699 the granaries, standing since before a' Scaradh, were pulled down and built again in dressed stone on raised floors against the rats, under the reeve Fearchar mac Phàdraig. Eight centuries after that a young clerk found the town's firlot worn smaller than the capital's standard, and had been for generations.
67.known_for: the barred granary, and the worn firlot

32.history: The walled ford town on the river above the granaries keeps the old crossing of the eastern road. In LE 554 Dùghall Garbh, guided by drovers who had used a hidden ford above the town for forty years to move cattle untolled, crossed his host in the dark and broke Raghnall Ruadh's camp at the ford; Leabhar a' Chùraim counts some three hundred dead, most of them drowned, and one old soldier swore to Seònaid nic Coinnich that the fighting took two days, not one. In the seventeenth century the growers on the slopes above the ford began to press blaeberry and bramble into a dark wine that kept a year in the cask, and the road-houses of the eastern stretch took to serving it as black wine.
32.known_for: the ford of Cogadh nan Trì Tagraichean, and the black wine

297.history: The long walled city on its ridge south of the capital was granted a market at every full moon by Queen Sìleas in LE 287, with a tally-house for the south, the first market right cut on paired sticks. At its first full-moon market traders came from three days' walk in every direction and carried honey, hemp, wax and pottery north as one company, and a trader of the long city asked the capital's clerk what stopped a false notch being cut after a bargain, and was shown how the grain of a split stick runs true only when its two halves are laid together.
297.known_for: the full-moon market and the paired tallies

316.history: The granary village on the road south of the ford had given carts and coal to Taigh na Fèithe without complaint for as long as anyone remembered, and did nothing to deserve what it got in LE 555, save stand on the road Raghnall Ruadh's broken host had to pass. The retreating men took what grain the granary held, fired it and a dozen houses about it, and went on. Coinneach mac Ailein carried his daughter Seònaid and the year's seed-corn out of the fire. Forty-one households walked six days south and wintered at Cathair mhòr on the charity of Macha's temple, where the fire went out in the winter of the refusal; Seònaid grew up to write Leabhar nan Trì Tagraichean. The village was rebuilt, and its people kept the tale of Na Teallaichean Fuara longer than any other in the island.
316.known_for: the burning of LE 555, and the child who wrote its history

360.history: The small mill town under Dùn chrom saw the last battle of Cogadh nam Bràithrean in LE 1,274, when Iain Ciar defeated his brother Alasdair Bàn below it, took him alive and let his captains go home. An ox-driver who turned back from the mountain road rather than push his team through unsettled country carried word of it to An Taigh-seinnse Mòr within the week, and could not say where the brothers now stood to one another; the peace was made two years later at the road-house.
360.known_for: the battle that ended Cogadh nam Bràithrean

318.history: The walled temple town in the middle country was seized by Alasdair Bàn's men in LE 1,270 and taken back by Iain Ciar. Na Seachd Taighean divided four to three over the brothers, and Cogadh nam Bràithrean is counted from this fight. Both households set every road between the two halves of the island under one following's watch or the other, and carters who had crossed freely all their lives had to say plainly whose peace they travelled under.
318.known_for: the first battle of Cogadh nam Bràithrean

30.history: The walled harbour city declared for Iain Ciar in Cogadh nam Bràithrean, and in LE 1,272 Alasdair Bàn's ships came down the coast and burned its waterfront before the town's own bell had finished ringing the alarm. The fire took the tarred rope stores and then the granary; by the second morning the town had lost both what it needed to put to sea and what it needed to eat until harvest. Cathair mhòr, which had taken no side, sent grain enough that no household went hungry that winter. In LE 1,549 a second great fire burned it with no war to blame, and before the ash had cooled its reeve ordered it rebuilt with gable walls of stone between each house and the next, so that a fire must cross stone to spread.
30.known_for: its two fires, and the gable walls

23.history: The walled market city of the south took in forty-one burnt-out households of Doire mhin in LE 555 at the temple of Macha and fed them through the winter on the temple's grain without asking whose claim they had favoured. In the winter of the refusal its temple fire went out in Dubhlas, on a morning so still the smoke of the last coals stood upright, and when a carrier's basket brought coal again it was the first of the cold shires' hearths to burn. Its market drew the trade of all the south, and a carter asked why he sold his barley here and not at the capital said a man carries his load to whichever gate opens first and pays best; by LE 969 it was greater than the capital. Its copper-workers stamped every cooking pot with a maker's mark and sent them out on every road. It fed Ceann mhin after the burning of Cogadh nam Bràithrean, and in the fifteenth century the priests of Macha finished their great house here, its floor of black and white eleven years in the laying, the largest roofed building on Dia-thìr.
23.known_for: Macha's great house, and the copper pots of every hearth

36.history: The harbour town on the south coast below the mountain finished its stone mole in LE 899, and the coal-barges of the mountain roads tied up there where before they had beached on shingle at low water; it became the port of the coal-carts coming down to the coast towns of the south. After Cogadh nam Bràithrean Alasdair Bàn held its lordship for life under the peace, kept the peace he had made to the end of his days, and died here in LE 1,291. The lordship returned to the crown, and Iain Ciar left it vacant for the rest of his reign.
36.known_for: the coal mole, and the lordship left vacant
